title: Enemies
hookLine: love your enemies, pray for those who persecute you
tomorrow: why does Jesus answer "who is my neighbor?" with a question?

cards: Someone posts a clip of your worst moment on purpose, captioned so you'll see it. The reply writes itself in your head.
Now a scene from the book of Acts, and it's a hard one, so gently: a man named Stephen has angered a crowd, and they drag him outside the city and begin to throw stones. He won't survive it.
At the edge of the crowd, the witnesses pile their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul, who approves of what they're doing.

teach.h: LAY NOT THIS SIN TO THEIR CHARGE.
teach.b: Here's who prays for the people throwing the stones. Stephen falls to his knees, and in the Douay-Rheims Bible he cries out with a loud voice: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." Then he dies.
If those words sound familiar, they should.
On the cross, Jesus says, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do."

teach.h: NOT LIKE THEM. PRAY FOR THEM.
teach.b: Stephen is doing what his teacher did, and what his teacher taught on the mountain: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you." Notice what's missing.
Jesus doesn't say like them. He doesn't say pretend it didn't happen, or stay where they can hurt you. He says pray for them.
It's the one thing you can do for an enemy that they can't stop and don't even have to know about. Now the cliffhanger.
Saul, the young man holding the coats, goes on to hunt Christians, until a light on the road to Damascus stops him.
He becomes Paul, the apostle whose letters are in the New Testament. Acts never says Stephen's prayer changed him.
It only puts the two of them in the same scene, the man praying and the man approving, and lets you wonder.

how: Catholics pray for enemies in their own prayers and in the Prayers of the Faithful at Mass, and the Church keeps the feast of Saint Stephen the day after Christmas.

o: people you're allowed to stop praying for
people who wish you harm, whom Jesus says to pray for
anyone who belongs to a different team or church

games.q: outside the city — tap the pairs.
p: lay not this sin to their charge

s: loving your enemies means you have to like them
Jesus says love, do good and pray; he doesn't say like them or pretend it didn't happen.
Stephen prayed for the crowd while they were stoning him
"Lord, lay not this sin to their charge."
Acts says Stephen's prayer is what converted Saul
Acts never says so. it only puts Saul in the scene, holding the coats.

games.q: a coworker took credit for your project in a meeting. that night you're still furious. what does Matthew 5:44 ask of you?
o: pray for him tonight, and still tell your boss the truth.
pretend it never happened and be extra nice tomorrow.
wait until the anger is gone, and then pray for him.
games.why: Jesus asks for prayer, not pretending. praying for an enemy can start while you're still angry, and it doesn't mean saying it was fine.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one person who has hurt you. Not the worst one; start small. Hold their face for a moment without rehearsing what they did.
If you pray, say Stephen's line for them: Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. If not, wish them one good thing, and mean as much of it as you can today.

wordCard.voice: Enemies. The people who wish you harm, and the people Jesus says to pray for anyway. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: pray for them. Stephen did it with the stones still coming. See you tomorrow.
